strengths: Well-motivated application domain: Applying 3D semantic scene completion (SSC) to legged and humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera directly tackles practical robotic constraints, such as 360-degree situational awareness, tight payload budgets, and gait-induced body jitter.

Valuable benchmark contributions: The paper introduces two dedicated panoramic occupancy benchmarks—QuadOcc (real-world quadruped with day/dusk/night splits and LiDAR-based ground truth) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based 360-degree human-ego simulation with gait)—which significantly facilitate future research in embodied panoramic perception.

Cohesive and well-tailored system design: The framework harmoniously combines Dual-Projection (DP-ER) to balance equator and polar distortions, Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) to marry Cartesian precision with camera-aligned cylindrical continuity, Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) to offset projection errors, and a Hierarchical AMoE-3D decoder.

Comprehensive empirical validation: OneOcc demonstrates consistent improvements over competitive vision-based baselines (e.g., +3.83 within-city and +8.08 cross-city mIoU on H3O; +1.37 mIoU on QuadOcc) and rivals/surpasses classic LiDAR-based approaches. Component ablations clearly demonstrate the progressive additive value of each module.
Clear runtime and efficiency profiling: The authors evaluate latency, memory footprint, and FP16 inference on edge/desktop hardware, demonstrating practical deployability on robotic platforms.
weaknesses: Conceptual ambiguity in Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC): Equation (9) regresses a single 2D translation offset (dx, dy) per feature scale from a single image via Global Average Pooling without temporal inputs or IMU sensor readings. Since gait jitter is fundamentally a dynamic, inter-frame temporal phenomenon, it is unclear how a single static frame determines gait-induced phase offsets rather than simply learning a global pitch/roll leveling bias relative to gravity. Further clarification or temporal ablation is needed.

Coarse voxel resolution for robotic locomotion: The occupancy grid resolution of 64x64x8 with 0.4 m voxels is relatively coarse for fine-grained quadruped foothold selection and obstacle negotiation (where obstacles < 10 cm can trip a legged robot). While acceptable as a baseline SSC formulation, its sufficiency for downstream locomotion planning warrants deeper discussion.

Presentation flaws and unpolished text: (1) In the abstract, the final sentence abruptly ends: 'Datasets and code will be publicly available at'; (2) In Figure 2, there is untranslated Chinese text ('极坐标转笛卡尔坐标') between the decoder blocks. These errors should be carefully fixed in the final manuscript.

strengths: Targets an important and underexplored problem in embodied 3D perception: semantic scene completion (SSC) specifically tailored for dynamic legged/humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera under gait-induced body jitter.

The proposed architectural components are well-motivated by domain geometry: Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) couples Cartesian and cylindrical-polar spaces to align with panoramic equirectangular geometry while maintaining metric precision for near-field contact geometry; DP-ER leverages both raw annular and unfolded representations.

Introduces two new panoramic SSC benchmarks: QuadOcc (real quadruped dataset with 10 scenes, 24K frames across day/dusk/night) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based 16-map benchmark with standardized within-city and cross-city splits).

Provides thorough empirical comparisons against adapted vision and LiDAR baselines, achieving competitive results on QuadOcc (+1.37 mIoU over MonoScene, outperforming LiDAR baselines) and substantial gains on H3O cross-city generalization (+8.08 mIoU over MonoScene).

Good operational efficiency with modest memory footprint (1.49-1.86 GB peak CUDA memory) and real-time execution (~18.9 FPS under mixed precision on an RTX 4090), supporting practical onboard deployment.
weaknesses: The Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) mechanism is modeled very simply as a single global 2D shift (dx, dy) regressed via Global Average Pooling and a linear layer per scale. Real quadruped locomotion causes complex 6-DoF angular and translational body jitter, which induces spatially non-uniform displacement across an omnidirectional 360-degree field of view. The paper lacks empirical analysis, trajectory error comparison, or visualization of what (dx, dy) actually learns.

Ablation gains on QuadOcc (Table 4) are relatively incremental for each introduced module: +0.39 mIoU for GDC, +0.31 mIoU for DP-ER, +0.41 mIoU for BGV, and +0.26 mIoU for AMoE-3D, totaling a 1.37 mIoU increase over the baseline.

The real-world QuadOcc benchmark is relatively constrained in semantic granularity (6 coarse semantic categories) and vertical resolution (64x64x8 grid, 0.4 m voxels, spanning only 3.2 m vertically). More details regarding semi-automatic annotation fidelity and temporal consistency across aggressive gait motions should be provided.
On QuadOcc under night conditions (Table 5), OneOcc lags behind MonoScene (13.50 vs. 14.20 mIoU), indicating sensitivity to low-light noise and limited annular texture visibility.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: 3D semantic scene completion tailored to legged/humanoid robots addresses key challenges absent in autonomous driving pipelines, specifically severe gait-induced jitter and the need for full 360-degree situational awareness under strict compute/sensor constraints.

Well-designed, domain-specific architecture: The combination of Dual-Projection fusion (DP-ER), Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV), and Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) effectively resolves the optical distortion trade-offs of panoramic lenses and aligns near-field Cartesian accuracy with far-field polar continuity.

Valuable benchmark contributions: The release of QuadOcc (real-world quadruped with day/dusk/night splits) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based 360 simulation across 16 maps with within- and cross-city splits) addresses a distinct lack of panoramic occupancy benchmarks in the robotics community.

Solid empirical performance and ablations: OneOcc outperforms leading vision baselines (e.g., +1.37 mIoU on QuadOcc and +8.08 mIoU cross-city on H3O over MonoScene) and rivals LiDAR baselines. The ablation study clearly breaks down the incremental value of each architectural component.
weaknesses: Simplistic formulation of gait compensation: GDC regresses a single global 2D displacement vector (dx, dy) via GAP and a linear layer. Legged locomotion induces complex 3D pitch, roll, and non-rigid optical displacement across panoramic projections, meaning a spatially uniform 2D shift is an oversimplification. An empirical comparison or discussion contrasting GDC with IMU-based or spatially-varying compensation would strengthen the claim.

Limited real-world dataset scale and diversity: QuadOcc is recorded in a single campus environment with 10 scenes, 6 semantic classes, and a relatively coarse 64x64x8 grid (0.4m voxels). While adequate as an initial robotic benchmark, the scale and structural diversity remain limited.

Degradation under low-light conditions: In Table 5, OneOcc's performance at night (13.50 mIoU) falls behind MonoScene (14.20 mIoU), indicating that the multi-stream/polar lifting mechanism may be more susceptible to high sensor noise and low visual contrast.

Lack of onboard edge-device benchmarks: The latency (~14-19 FPS) is measured on a high-end desktop GPU (RTX 4090). While the paper presents theoretical TFLOPS scaling for Jetson Thor, actual execution benchmarks on embedded compute platforms commonly mounted on quadruped robots (such as Jetson Orin) are missing.

strengths: Addresses an important and under-explored problem: 3D semantic scene completion tailored specifically for legged and humanoid platforms using a single panoramic camera, tackling specific challenges such as gait-induced body jitter and 360-degree azimuthal continuity under tight onboard compute budgets.

Well-motivated architectural contributions tailored to panoramic geometry: Dual-Projection (DP-ER) balances annular optics and equirectangular representations; Bi-Grid Voxelization (BGV) bridges near-field Cartesian contact geometry with far-field cylindrical azimuthal continuity; Hierarchical AMoE-3D provides dynamic, edge-aware feature aggregation; and Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC) cheaply stabilizes lifting against motion shake.

Valuable dataset contributions: Introduces two panoramic occupancy benchmarks—QuadOcc (real quadruped multi-sensor data with a semi-automatic labeling pipeline across day/dusk/night) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based 360-degree human-ego simulation across 16 maps, multiple weathers, and simulated gait bobbing).

Thorough evaluation and real-world deployment considerations: Provides extensive benchmarking against both vision and classical LiDAR baselines, detailed ablations, calibration robustness tests, FoV scaling, and on-device latency profiling on an NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.
weaknesses: Coarse voxel resolution: The primary grid resolution is 64x64x8 (0.4 m voxels), which is relatively coarse for precise foothold planning or detecting small obstacles critical to legged locomotion. Although the authors analyze a 128x128x16 resolution in the supplementary material, performance drops substantially (mIoU drops from 32.23 to 21.16 on H3O), highlighting difficulties in training and optimizing at higher granularities.

Simplified gait compensation model: GDC regresses a single global 2D offset Delta = (dx, dy) per feature scale via global average pooling. However, dynamic legged locomotion typically induces 6-DoF oscillations (roll, pitch, yaw, and translation), which create spatially varying displacement fields across panoramic equirectangular / annular projections rather than a uniform 2D translation.

Modest gains on certain classes in the real benchmark: In QuadOcc (Table 2), the margin over MonoScene is relatively modest (+1.37 mIoU overall, 20.56 vs. 19.19), with dominant categories like road and vegetation exhibiting marginal differences.

Limited real-world diversity: QuadOcc is confined to a single campus domain with 10 scenes and a 6-class taxonomy. While H3O adds cross-city diversity, it relies purely on CARLA simulation, leaving real humanoid deployment and sim-to-real transfer as open questions.

strengths: Compelling problem formulation: Adapting 3D semantic scene completion to legged and humanoid robots using a single panoramic camera directly tackles the practical embodied challenges of severe gait-induced camera jitter, omnidirectional coverage, and strict compute/payload budgets.

Technically coherent architecture tailored to panoramic imaging: The combination of Dual-Projection (DP-ER), Bi-Grid Voxelization (Cartesian for near-field contact and Cylindrical for far-field panoramic alignment), Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC), and 3D Attention-MoE effectively addresses distortion and jitter without requiring extra inertial/proprioceptive sensors.

Release of two specialized benchmarks: Both QuadOcc (real quadruped multi-lighting dataset with synchronized LiDAR ground truth) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based 16-map simulation with multiple weathers/times) provide valuable testbeds for panoramic embodied occupancy.

Exemplary experimental thoroughness and ablation study: The paper includes extensive ablations on module contributions, horizontal FoV variation, bi-grid components, number of MoE experts, calibration noise sensitivity, temporal aggregation, and actual edge runtime benchmarks on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin.
weaknesses: Coarse voxel resolution: The primary grid resolution is 64x64x8 at 0.4 m per voxel. While practical for real-time edge hardware, 0.4 m is relatively coarse for precise legged locomotion (e.g., small footholds, curbs, and thin obstacles). When scaling to 128x128x16, performance drops significantly (from 32.23 to 21.16 mIoU on H3O), showing that the pipeline struggles under fine discretizations.

Real-world benchmark scale and taxonomy: QuadOcc comprises 10 scenes in a campus environment with a coarse 6-class taxonomy. While practical, the dataset size is somewhat limited compared to automotive benchmarks.

Reliance on 2D vision foundation models for real ground truth: The QuadOcc ground-truth annotation relies heavily on Grounded-SAM 2D segmentation transferred to LiDAR points with semi-automatic refinement, which could introduce systematic semantic labeling errors or transfer biases.

strengths: Compelling and well-motivated problem formulation: While most 3D semantic scene completion (SSC) methods focus on forward-facing cameras on wheeled vehicles, this work targets single panoramic camera perception on dynamic legged/humanoid robots, directly addressing payload constraints, gait-induced body jitter, and 360-degree situational awareness.

Well-tailored technical contributions: The individual components (Dual-Projection DP-ER, Bi-Grid Voxelization BGV combining Cartesian and polar spaces, and Gait Displacement Compensation GDC) are specifically engineered to handle panoramic optical distortions and camera oscillation during locomotion.

Comprehensive benchmark contributions: The paper introduces two complementary benchmarks—QuadOcc (real quadruped dataset with time-synchronized LiDAR ground-truth generation) and Human360Occ (CARLA-based human-ego dataset across 16 maps with simulated gait dynamics and weather variations).

Extensive experimental validation and ablations: The evaluation covers comparisons with strong vision-based and LiDAR-based SSC baselines, detailed ablations on field-of-view scaling (90° to 360°), calibration robustness, voxel resolution scaling, and real embedded runtime benchmarks on NVIDIA Jetson AGX Orin (demonstrating ~13.6 FPS onboard).
weaknesses: Coarse voxel resolution and vertical discretization: The default grid is 64x64x8 with 0.4m voxels, leaving only 8 bins along the vertical axis over a 3.2m range. As shown in the authors' resolution scaling experiments, scaling to 128x128x16 causes a significant drop in mIoU, which limits fine-grained geometric perception for detailed foothold selection or manipulation.

Simplicity of Gait Displacement Compensation (GDC): GDC regresses a single global 2D offset (dx, dy) per feature scale via global average pooling and a linear layer. Because 3D rotational jitter (roll, pitch, yaw) on a 360° panoramic camera induces spatially varying, non-uniform displacements rather than a uniform 2D shift, the modeling capacity of a single global 2D translation may be overly simplified.

Dataset scale and GT label noise on QuadOcc: QuadOcc contains 10 sequences collected within a single campus environment with only 6 classes. Furthermore, ground-truth semantics are derived semi-automatically using Grounded-SAM pseudo-labels projected onto accumulated LiDAR scans, which inherently inherits 2D model labeling errors and boundary ambiguities.

Discrepancy in method configuration across benchmarks: Because Human360Occ synthesizes native equirectangular panoramas, the raw-annulus branch of DP-ER is disabled on H3O, meaning the full dual-projection pipeline is only evaluated on QuadOcc.
